result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.count_loops()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Count self-loops grouped by node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L61756-L61842){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.count_loops() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Count loops per node](/assets/graphs/count-loops.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Four nodes in a row, A to D, with node ids 1 to 4 below them. Node A carries two self-loops and node C one, all in the accent color. The card maps node id to loop count: node 3 has 1 and node 1 has 2." width="100%"} Returns a dictionary mapping node IDs to the count of self-loops for each node. Only includes nodes that have at least one self-loop. Where `which_loops()` lists the individual self-loop edges, this method tallies them per node. That is handy for: - finding which nodes have self-loops, and how many, in one call - spotting nodes with suspiciously many self-loops after a data import - building a node attribute from the counts (pass the dictionary to `set_node_attrs()`) The graph is not modified, and both directed and undirected graphs are supported. To delete self-loops, use `remove_selfloops()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping node IDs to self-loop counts. Only includes nodes with count `>= 1`, so an empty dictionary means the graph has no self-loops. The order of entries is not meaningful. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Groups the flat list from `which_loops()` by node in a single $O(E)$ pass, returning only nodes with at least one self-loop and reporting the exact per-node count. A node may accumulate several self-loops in a multigraph, for instance an autocatalytic species with multiple self-referencing reactions in a chemical network, or a state in an automaton with several distinct "no-op" transitions, and the reported multiplicity reflects that. The complementary primitive is `which_loops()`, which returns the flat edge-ID list without grouping. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes can have more than one self-loop, so this groups the count by node rather than returning a flat list of edges. Here `A` has two loops, `B` has one, and `C` and `D` are absent because they have none: ::: {#1853319d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "A"), # Self-loop ("A", "A"), # Another self-loop ("B", "B"), # Self-loop ("C", "D"), # No self-loop ] ) loop_counts = g.count_loops() # Returns {'A': 2, 'B': 1} {g.get_label_from_id(nid): count for nid, count in sorted(loop_counts.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 2, 'B': 1} ``` ::: ::: In a chemical reaction network, this can highlight autocatalytic species -- ones that catalyze their own production through one or more self-referencing pathways: ::: {#d9f4c412 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} rxn = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "B"), # B catalyzes itself ("B", "B"), # Multiple pathways ("C", "C"), # C is autocatalytic ] ) ) autocatalytic = rxn.count_loops() # Returns {'B': 2, 'C': 1} {rxn.get_label_from_id(nid): count for nid, count in sorted(autocatalytic.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'B': 2, 'C': 1} ``` ::: :::
